official_measurement_examples.fact: A planning application is not valid unless the relevant ownership certificate and agricultural land declaration requirements are satisfied.
Certificate A is only for sole ownership with no agricultural tenants; B, C and D cover differing knowledge of other owners or agricultural tenants.
For this purpose an owner includes a freeholder or a leaseholder with at least seven years unexpired term.
Applicants may apply for planning permission on land they do not own, provided the statutory certificate and notice requirements are met.
False or misleading ownership certificates can constitute an offence; the certificate is a statutory declaration mechanism rather than title adjudication.
Certificates C and D require publication/notice steps where some or all owners are unknown, subject to the prescribed process.
Appeal ownership certificates use related ownership/notice concepts but an appeal certificate does not cure an invalid original application automatically.
Ownership certificate status does not establish registered title boundaries, access rights, planning acceptability, infrastructure capacity or development yield.

core_rules: Certificate A requires sole ownership and no agricultural tenant
B C D reflect different owner knowledge
seven-year lease definition must be retained
notice service is distinct from ownership proof
false certificate risk must be retained
certificate validity is distinct from planning merits
appeal certificate is not original-application cure
certificate does not establish access rights
certificate does not establish cadastral boundary
certificate does not prove infrastructure capacity
application date and ownership snapshot matter
no parcel ownership clearance or Future Growth score may be promoted while recovery is parked
